title: Cytotoxic Drugs
path: Drugs Used for Conditions Apart from Systemic Disorders

headings.title: Introduction and Mechanism of Action
headings.content: Cytotoxic drugs are potent pharmacological agents utilized primarily to treat malignant neoplasms by halting cellular proliferation. Their primary mode of action targets rapidly dividing cells, interfering with various stages of the cell cycle. Because cancer cells replicate uncontrollably, they are exceptionally vulnerable to these disruptions compared to most resting normal cells. However, normal tissues with high physiological turnover—such as the bone marrow, hair follicles, and gastrointestinal epithelium—are also severely affected, leading to characteristic side effects.

headings.title: Classification of Cytotoxic Agents
headings.content:
Pharmacologists classify cytotoxic drugs based on their biochemical interaction with cellular replication. Understanding these classes helps clinicians predict specific toxicities and design combination therapy regimens.

- **Alkylating agents**: Directly cross-link DNA strands, preventing proper unwinding and replication.
- **Antimetabolites**: Mimic essential cellular metabolites, substituting themselves into DNA or RNA synthesis pathways.
- **Antitumor antibiotics**: Bind to DNA and inhibit enzymes necessary for nucleic acid synthesis.
- **Plant alkaloids**: Disrupt mitotic spindle formation during cell division, arresting mitosis.

headings.title: Clinical Indications Beyond Oncology
headings.content:
While primarily recognized for treating solid tumors and hematological malignancies, cytotoxic drugs also play a vital role in managing severe non-malignant conditions. Their ability to suppress aberrant immune system activity makes them valuable in treating autoimmune diseases and preventing solid organ transplant rejection.

- **Rheumatoid Arthritis**: Methotrexate reduces chronic joint inflammation and slows structural damage.
- **Systemic Lupus Erythematosus**: Cyclophosphamide controls severe organ-threatening autoimmune flares.
- **Organ Transplantation**: Azathioprine suppresses lymphocyte proliferation to prevent graft rejection.

headings.title: Routes of Administration and Safe Handling
headings.content:
Cytotoxic medications are administered through various routes including intravenous, oral, intrathecal, and subcutaneous pathways. Because these compounds are inherently hazardous, healthcare personnel must strictly adhere to safety protocols to prevent occupational exposure.

| Safety Measure | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| **Double-gloving** | Prevents skin absorption through microscopic tears |
| **Chemotherapy gown** | Protects the torso and arms from splashes or aerosols |
| **Closed-system transfer devices** | Minimizes drug vapor escape during preparation |
| **Dedicated disposal bins** | Contains cytotoxic waste for high-temperature incineration |

headings.title: Adverse Effects and Toxicity Profiles
headings.content: The toxicity profile of cytotoxic drugs reflects their indiscriminate effect on rapidly proliferating normal tissues. Bone marrow suppression leads to neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and anemia. Gastrointestinal toxicities manifest as severe mucositis, nausea, and persistent vomiting. Certain specific agents carry unique organ-specific risks, such as doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity and cisplatin-induced nephrotoxicity or ototoxicity.

headings.title: Pre-Administration Assessment
headings.content: Comprehensive baseline assessment before administering cytotoxic therapy ensures patient safety and helps guide dosage adjustments. Nurses must evaluate complete blood count values to ensure bone marrow recovery from previous cycles. Renal and hepatic function panels are mandatory since most of these drugs are metabolized or excreted through the liver and kidneys. Furthermore, assessing the patient's hydration status, baseline weight, and functional performance score helps detect early signs of intolerance.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions for Complications
headings.content: Managing complications arising from cytotoxic therapy requires prompt clinical intervention. For myelosuppression, strict infection control measures and prompt administration of colony-stimulating factors are vital. Antiemetic medications should be given proactively before nausea begins rather than reactively after symptoms start. For extravasation—the accidental leakage of vesicant drugs into surrounding subcutaneous tissue—the infusion must be stopped immediately, and specific antidotes or cold/warm compresses applied according to facility protocol.

headings.title: Patient and Caregiver Home Care Education
headings.content: Patients discharged home during or after cytotoxic therapy require clear guidance to manage side effects safely and recognize red flag symptoms. Education must cover personal hygiene, safe food preparation to avoid foodborne illness during periods of neutropenia, and proper handling of body excretions. Caregivers should be taught when to contact the clinical team immediately, particularly if the patient develops a fever, unusual bleeding, or severe dehydration.
